records.quote:
she told me that all the people whom I had seen had died of fever. When
they had died the other inhabitants of the kraal had taken the cattle
and gone away, leaving the poor old woman
records.paraphrase: An entire village has been wiped out by fever, leaving only one old woman.

records.quote:
there I lay shaking
with terror, and the cold perspiration pouring out of me
records.paraphrase: The narrator describes his terror while lions feed near him.

records.quote:
It was, I think, in the March of '69 that I was up in Sikukuni's
country.
records.paraphrase: The narrator sets the tale in a specific past year and remote African locale.

records.quote:
He is persuaded that a white people, of which he
has heard rumours all his life, exists somewhere on the highlands in the
vast, still unexplored interior
records.paraphrase: The framing describes a quest into an unexplored interior for a rumored hidden white people.

records.quote:
the first thing I set to work to do was to try to
discover whereabouts the brutes lay up for the day
records.paraphrase: The hunter systematically investigates where the lions rest during the day.

records.quote:
The lion is soft, and not a difficult animal
to finish if you hit him anywhere in the body. A buck takes far more
killing.
records.paraphrase: Quatermain gives a practical explanation of a lion's vulnerability compared to a buck.

records.quote:
when I tried to get in the new
cartridge it would only enter half-way
records.paraphrase: A burst cartridge case fouls the breech so a new round won't seat, explaining the gun's failure.

records.quote:
I have been lame ever
since, and shall be to my dying day; in the month of March the wound
always troubles me a great deal, and every three years it breaks out
raw.
records.paraphrase: The lasting injury permanently marks the narrator's body.

records.quote:
It was the fever mist. Out from among the
scrub, too, came little spirals of vapour, as though there were hundreds
of tiny fires alight in it--reek rising from thousands of tons of
rotting vegetation.
records.paraphrase: The narrator explains the mist as fever vapor rising from rotting vegetation.

records.quote:
there was a
strong wind blowing from the direction of the waggon, across the reedy
pan towards the bush-clad kloof or donga, and this first gave me the
idea of firing the reeds
records.paraphrase: He reasons from wind direction to devise a plan to burn out the lions.

records.quote:
the death of his only son so unsettled him that he immediately
left England
records.paraphrase: Quatermain is deeply affected by his son's death and abandons England.

records.quote:
Those people carry the doctrine of the survival of
the fittest to its extreme, you see.
records.paraphrase: The narrator contrasts native practice with a scientific-sounding principle for the reader.

criteria.rationale: The story offers only ordinary period observations: fever mist as vapor from rotting vegetation, and a colloquial reference to 'survival of the fittest.' These are folk explanations and a passing phrase, not a materially represented scientific fact, theory, discovery, or speculative science. No scientific concept drives the narrative, which is a straightforward hunting adventure.

The firearms (a No. 12 smoothbore breechloader) and a burst cartridge case are ordinary contemporary tools of the period. Although the cartridge jam creates dramatic tension, a mundane rifle malfunction is an incidental hazard, not an engineered system, technique, or invention that constitutes a speculative or materially novel technology in the science-fiction sense.

The tale is set in 1869 South Africa, a recent historical past relative to its telling, with an incidental date. There is no speculative future, remote past, or temporal displacement; the setting is an ordinary historical/geographic frame for a retrospective yarn.

The narrator's reasoning about wind direction to fire the reeds is ordinary practical bushcraft, not the systematic development of consequences from an identifiable scientific, technological, social, or historical premise. Nothing in the story extrapolates a premise into extended consequences characteristic of science fiction.

The hunter observes tracks and kill remains, forms the hypothesis that the lions lie up in the pan, tests it, and reasons from wind direction to plan the fire. This is systematic inference and observation driving action, but it amounts to ordinary practical tracking rather than a scientific method materially central to understanding; hence ambiguous with incidental materiality.

The framing mentions a rumored hidden white people in unexplored African interior, but this is an ordinary earthly locale and legend, not another planet, dimension, nonordinary cosmic environment, or visitors from such. No such element appears in the actual narrated story.

A widespread fever epidemic that year has depopulated a kraal, wiping out an entire village and leaving one dying survivor, and the whole region 'reeked of fever'—a biological disaster of some scale that is remembered and sets the atmosphere. However it is background context rather than causally central to the lion-hunt plot, so it is ambiguous with incidental materiality.

candidates.description: A rumored hidden white civilization existing somewhere on the highlands of the vast, unexplored African interior, framed as the object of Quatermain's final quest.

novelty.rationale: A lost/hidden race would constitute a world-altering difference from the empirical norm if realized, but the story presents it only as an unverified rumor in the frame; it never enters the narrative as an actualized world-difference.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The hidden people are offered as a naturalistic (nonsupernatural) geographic/anthropological possibility consistent with lost-race conventions, but no systematic account of them is given in this text.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The rumored people appear only in the framing preface and do not govern the narrative logic; the actual told story is entirely a realistic lion-hunting adventure with no bearing on the hidden race.

estrangement.rationale: The frame gestures toward a marvelous discovery beyond the known map, contrasting the mundane empirical world with a possible hidden civilization, but this is never developed into an operative world-difference within the story.

candidates.description: The core action of a solitary hunter confronting a family of lions in the African bush, including the burning-out tactic and the near-fatal mauling.

novelty.rationale: Lion hunting and gun malfunctions are entirely within the authorial empirical norm; nothing here totalizes or alters the story universe. It is a realistic adventure, not a science-fictional difference.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The hunting logic (lion vulnerability, cartridge fouling, wind-driven fire) is coherent and naturalistic, but coherence alone does not create a novum absent novelty.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: This action dominates and determines the entire told narrative, but centrality of an ordinary adventure element does not qualify it as a novum.

estrangement.rationale: There is no cognitive estrangement: the events are consistent with the ordinary empirical world of 19th-century African hunting, with no world-altering difference for the reader to reconcile.
